newsitem.title: USA: Currency peg still useful in E.Europe--IMF.
newsitem.headline: Currency peg still useful in E.Europe--IMF.

text.p: Transitional economies should be wary of giving up the currency anchor used to bring inflation down, but may need to be flexible before there are signs of a crisis, a senior IMF official said on Monday.

IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer told a news briefing that Poland had acted very intelligently to cope with possible problems, moving rapidly to a crawling peg and widening the currency's trading bands.

"That is the sort of thing that needs to be done before the crunch," Fischer said. "But I am reluctant to just tell countries like that which use the exchange rate as an anchor to bring inflation down to give it up."
He said currency anchors had brought benefits to many countries in terms of lowering inflation, although a floating rate might be less of a target for speculators.
Some markets worried about the stability of currencies in eastern Europe after Thailand was forced to devalue the baht.

Many of these countries have pegged their currency against the mark, the dollar or against a basket of currencies in an effort to force inflation down, but policies range from an inflexible currency board to a relatively wide band of permissable currency fluctuation within a sloping corridor.
